t:
(a) Administrative Subpoenas.—
        (1) In general.—Section 3486(a)(1) of title 18, United States Code, is amended—
            (A) in subparagraph (A)—
                (i) in clause (i), by striking “or” at the end; 
                (ii) by redesignating clause (ii) as clause (iii); and 
                (iii) by inserting after clause (i) the following:“(ii) an unregistered sex offender conducted by the United States Marshals Service, the Director of the United States Marshals Service; or”; and  
            (B) in subparagraph (D)—
                (i) by striking “paragraph, the term” and inserting the following: “paragraph—“(i) the term”; 
                (ii) by striking the period at the end and inserting “; and”; and 
                (iii) by adding at the end the following:“(ii) the term ‘sex offender’ means an individual required to register under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (42 U.S.C. 16901 et seq.).”.   
        (2) Technical and conforming amendments.—Section 3486(a) of title 18, United States Code, is amended—
            (A) in paragraph (6)(A), by striking “United State” and inserting “United States”; 
            (B) in paragraph (9), by striking “(1)(A)(ii)” and inserting “(1)(A)(iii)”; and 
            (C) in paragraph (10), by striking “paragraph (1)(A)(ii)” and inserting “paragraph (1)(A)(iii)”.   
    (b) Judicial Subpoenas.—Section 566(e)(1) of title 28, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) in subparagraph (A), by striking “and” at the end; 
        (2) in subparagraph (B), by striking the period at the end and inserting “; and”; and 
        (3) by adding at the end the following:“(C) issue administrative subpoenas in accordance with section 3486 of title 18, solely for the purpose of investigating unregistered sex offenders (as defined in such section 3486).”.

fable.w: The section amends federal law to let the U.S. Marshals Service issue administrative subpoenas when investigating unregistered sex offenders. The tempting reading is that subpoenas involve outside parties, but a subpoena compels information for a law-enforcement investigation; it does not consult outsiders or invite their input before a federal decision. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, consultation with non-federal entities, or right to sue.
fable.s: issue administrative subpoenas in accordance with section 3486 of title 18, solely for the purpose of investigating unregistered sex offenders

qwen_block.w: This section amends statutes to grant the United States Marshals Service and federal courts the authority to issue administrative subpoenas for investigating unregistered sex offenders. It does not require consultation, coordination, or participation with outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) in making a decision. The issuance of a subpoena is an enforcement or investigative tool, not a participatory process involving external stakeholders in decision-making.
qwen_block.s: issue administrative subpoenas in accordance with section 3486 of title 18, solely for the purpose of investigating unregistered sex offenders

opus.w: This section gives the U.S. Marshals Service subpoena power to investigate unregistered sex offenders, and the rest is technical and conforming amendments. A subpoena is a federal enforcement tool that forces people to produce evidence. It does not bring states, experts, the public or other outsiders into a federal policy decision. There is also no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation requirement or right to sue in this text.
opus.s: (C) issue administrative subpoenas in accordance with section 3486 of title 18, solely for the purpose of investigating unregistered sex offenders (as defined in such section 3486).
opus.b: The tempting reading is "Yes": subpoenas compel people outside the government to hand over information, and the existing section 3486 lets a subpoena recipient go to court to challenge it. That reading fails. Being compelled to produce evidence in a law-enforcement investigation is not consulting with the government before a policy decision. This text also doesn't grant any right to comment, consult or sue over a decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the issuance of administrative subpoenas for investigative purposes. It does not require the government to consult with, coordinate with, or seek advice from outside parties before making a decision. The interaction described is coercive (subpoena) rather than participatory (consultation/advisory). Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_chat.s: issue administrative subpoenas in accordance with section 3486 of title 18, solely for the purpose of investigating unregistered sex offenders
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the ability to issue subpoenas to unregistered sex offenders constitutes "participation" because it involves interaction with outside parties. However, the definition of participation requires consultation, coordination, or advisory input *before* a decision is made, or the granting of a right to sue/object. Issuing a subpoena is an enforcement or investigative tool used by the government to compel information; it is not a mechanism for the outside party to participate in the decision-making process. The outside party is being compelled to provide information, not consulted or invited to advise.
